blocks.p: Man’s transgression becomes known. The guardian angels leave Paradise and return up to Heaven to show that they kept watch faithfully, and are approved, God declaring that they could not have prevented Satan’s entrance. He sends his Son to judge the transgressors; the Son descends and gives sentence accordingly, then in pity clothes them both, and goes back up. Sin and Death, who until then sat at the gates of Hell, feel by a wondrous sympathy Satan’s success in this new world and the sin Man has committed there, and resolve to sit confined in Hell no longer, but to follow Satan, their father, up to the place of Man. To make the way between Hell and this world easier in both directions, they pave a broad highway or bridge over Chaos, along the track Satan first made. Then, as they set out for Earth, they meet him returning to Hell, proud of his success, and they congratulate one another. Satan arrives at Pandaemonium and, before the full assembly, boastfully relates his success against Man. Instead of applause he is met with a general hiss from all his audience, who are suddenly transformed, he along with them, into serpents, according to the sentence given him in Paradise. Then, deceived by an illusion of the forbidden tree springing up before them, they greedily reach to take the fruit, and chew dust and bitter ashes. The doings of Sin and Death follow. God foretells his Son’s final victory over them and the renewal of all things, but for the present commands his angels to make various alterations in the heavens and the elements. Adam, seeing his fallen condition more and more clearly, laments it heavily and rejects Eve’s attempts to comfort him. She persists, and at last calms him. Then, to escape the curse likely to fall on their offspring, she proposes violent ways to Adam, which he does not approve; but, conceiving a better hope, he reminds her of the promise lately made to them, that her seed would be avenged on the Serpent, and urges her to seek with him the peace of the offended Deity by repentance and prayer.

v: Meanwhile the heinous and malicious act
Of Satan done in Paradise, and how
He in the Serpent had perverted Eve,
And she her husband, to taste the fatal fruit,
Was known in Heaven; for what escapes the eye
Of God all-seeing, or deceives his heart
Omniscient, who, in all things wise and just,
Did not stop Satan from assailing the mind
Of Man, with strength entire and free will armed,
Complete to have discovered and repelled
Whatever wiles of foe or seeming friend.
For still they knew, and should have still remembered,
The high injunction not to taste that fruit,
Whoever tempted; which, not obeying, they
Incurred (what less could they?) the penalty,
And, manifold in sin, deserved to fall.
Up into Heaven from Paradise in haste
The angel guards ascended, mute and sad
For Man, for by this time they knew his state,
Much wondering how the subtle fiend had stolen
Entrance unseen. And when the unwelcome news
From Earth arrived at Heaven’s gate, displeased
Were all who heard; dim sadness did not spare
The faces of the angels then, yet, mixed
With pity, it did not violate their bliss.
Around the newly come, in multitudes
The ethereal people ran, to hear and know
How all befell. They to the throne supreme,
Accountable, made haste to make appear,
With righteous plea, their utmost vigilance,
And were easily approved; when the Most High,
Eternal Father, from his secret cloud,
Amid the thunder uttered thus his voice:
“Assembled angels, and you powers returned
From unsuccessful charge, do not be dismayed,
Nor troubled at these tidings from the Earth,
Which your sincerest care could not prevent,
Foretold so lately, what would come to pass
When first this tempter crossed the gulf from Hell.
I told you then he would prevail and speed
On his bad errand; Man would be seduced
And flattered out of all, believing lies
Against his Maker; no decree of mine
Concurring to necessitate his fall,
Or touch with lightest moment of impulse
His free will, to her own inclining left
In even scale. But fallen he is; and now
Nothing remains but that the sentence pass
On his transgression, death proclaimed that day,
Which he presumes already vain and void
Because not yet inflicted, as he feared,
By some immediate stroke, but soon shall find
Forbearance no acquittal, by day’s end.
Justice shall not return, as bounty, scorned.
But whom to send to judge them? Whom but you,
Vicegerent Son? To you I have transferred
All judgment, whether in Heaven, or Earth, or Hell.
It may be easily seen that I intend
Mercy as colleague with justice, sending you,
Man’s friend, his mediator, his designed
Both ransom and redeemer voluntary,
And destined Man himself to judge Man fallen.”
So spoke the Father, and, unfolding bright
Toward the right hand his glory, on the Son
Blazed forth unclouded deity; he, full
Resplendent, all his Father manifest
Expressed, and thus divinely answered mild:
“Father eternal, yours is to decree,
Mine, both in Heaven and Earth, to do your will
Supreme, that you in me, your Son beloved,
May always rest well pleased. I go to judge
On Earth these your transgressors; but you know,
Whoever is judged, the worst on me must light,
When time shall be; for so I undertook
Before you; and, regretting nothing, claim
This right, that I may mitigate their doom,
Transferred to me; yet I shall temper so
Justice with mercy as may best display
Both fully satisfied, and you appeased.
No escort shall I need, nor train, where none
Are to behold the judgment but the judged,
Those two; the third, best absent, is condemned,
Convicted by his flight, and rebel to law:
The Serpent has no need to be convicted.”
So saying, from his radiant seat he rose
Of high collateral glory; him Thrones and Powers,
Princedoms, and Dominations, ministering,
Accompanied to Heaven’s gate, from where
Eden and all the coast in prospect lay.
Down he descended straight; the speed of gods
Time cannot count, though winged with swiftest minutes.
Now was the sun in western cadence low
From noon, and gentle breezes, due at their hour
To fan the earth now waking, and usher in
The evening cool, when he, from wrath more cool,
Came, the mild Judge and Intercessor both,
To sentence Man. The voice of God they heard
Now walking in the garden, by soft winds
Brought to their ears, while day declined; they heard,
And from his presence hid themselves among
The thickest trees, both man and wife, till God,
Approaching, thus to Adam called aloud:
“Where are you, Adam, used to meet with joy
My coming, seen far off? I miss you here,
Not pleased to be received with solitude,
Where duty came to meet me once unsought.
Or do I come less noticed, or what change
Absents you, or what chance detains? Come forth.”
He came, and with him Eve, more loath, though first
To offend, abashed, and both of them distraught;
Love was not in their looks, either to God
Or to each other, but apparent guilt,
And shame, and perturbation, and despair,
Anger, and obstinacy, and hate, and guile.
And Adam, faltering long, thus briefly answered:
“I heard you in the garden, and, of your voice
Afraid, being naked, hid myself.” To whom
The gracious Judge without reproach replied:
“My voice you often heard, and did not fear,
But always rejoiced; how has it now become
So dreadful to you? That you are naked, who
Has told you? Have you eaten of the tree
Of which I gave you charge you should not eat?”
To whom thus Adam, sorely pressed, replied:
“O Heaven! In evil straits this day I stand
Before my Judge, either to undergo
Myself the total crime, or to accuse
My other self, the partner of my life,
Whose failing, while her faith to me remains,
I should conceal, and not expose to blame
By my complaint; but strict necessity
Subdues me, and calamitous constraint,
Lest on my head both sin and punishment,
However insupportable, be all
Devolved; though should I hold my peace, yet you
Would easily detect what I conceal.
This woman, whom you made to be my help,
And gave me as your perfect gift, so good,
So fit, so acceptable, so divine,
That from her hand I could suspect no ill,
And what she did, whatever in itself,
Her doing seemed to justify the deed:
She gave me of the tree, and I did eat.”
To whom the sovereign Presence thus replied:
“Was she your God, that you obeyed her word
Before his voice? Or was she made your guide,
Superior, or but equal, that to her
You should resign your manhood, and the place
In which God set you above her, made of you
And for you, whose perfection far excelled
Hers in all real dignity? Adorned
She was indeed, and lovely, to attract
Your love, not your subjection; and her gifts
Were such as under government looked well,
Unseemly to bear rule, which was your part
And office, had you rightly known yourself.”
So having said, he turned to Eve in brief:
“Say, woman, what is this that you have done?”
To whom sad Eve, with shame near overwhelmed,
Confessing soon, yet not before her Judge
Bold or loquacious, thus abashed replied:
“The Serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.”
Which when the Lord God heard, without delay
To judgment he proceeded on the accused
Serpent, though brute, unable to transfer
The guilt to him who made him instrument
Of mischief, and polluted from the end
Of his creation; justly, then, accursed,
As vitiated in nature. More to know
Concerned not Man (since he no further knew),
Nor altered his offense; yet God at last
To Satan, first in sin, his doom applied,
Though in mysterious terms, judged then as best;
And on the Serpent thus his curse let fall:
“Because you have done this, you are accursed
Above all cattle, each beast of the field;
Upon your belly groveling you shall go,
And dust shall eat all the days of your life.
Between you and the woman I will put
Enmity, and between your seed and hers;
Her seed shall bruise your head, you bruise his heel.”
So spoke this oracle, then verified
When Jesus, son of Mary, second Eve,
Saw Satan fall like lightning down from Heaven,
Prince of the air; then, rising from his grave,
Stripped principalities and powers, triumphed
In open show, and with ascension bright
Captivity led captive through the air,
The realm itself of Satan, long usurped,
Whom he shall tread at last beneath our feet;
Even he who now foretold his fatal bruise,
And to the woman thus his sentence turned:
“Your sorrow I will greatly multiply
By your conception; children you shall bring
In sorrow forth; and to your husband’s will
Yours shall submit; he over you shall rule.”
On Adam last thus judgment he pronounced:
“Because you listened to the voice of your wife,
And have eaten of the tree concerning which
I charged you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’
Cursed is the ground for your sake; you in sorrow
Shall eat of it all the days of your life;
Thorns also and thistles it shall bring you forth
Unbidden, and you shall eat the herb of the field;
In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread,
Until you return to the ground; for you
Out of the ground were taken: know your birth;
For dust you are, and shall to dust return.”
So he judged Man, both Judge and Savior sent,
And the instant stroke of death, pronounced that day,
Removed far off; then, pitying how they stood
Before him naked to the air, that now
Must suffer change, did not disdain to begin
From then the form of servant to assume,
As when he washed his servants’ feet; so now,
As father of his family, he clad
Their nakedness with skins of beasts, or slain,
Or, like the snake, with youthful coat repaid;
And did not grudge to clothe his enemies;
Nor only their outward selves with the skins
Of beasts, but inward nakedness, much more
Opprobrious, with his robe of righteousness
Arraying, covered from his Father’s sight.
To him with swift ascent he then returned,
Into his blissful bosom reassumed
In glory as of old; to him, appeased,
All, though all-knowing, what had passed with Man
Recounted, mixing intercession sweet.
Meanwhile, before this sin and doom on Earth,
Within the gates of Hell sat Sin and Death,
Each facing each, within the gates, that now
Stood open wide, belching outrageous flame
Far into Chaos, since the fiend passed through,
Sin opening; who now thus to Death began:
“O son, why sit here, each the other viewing,
Idly, while Satan, our great author, thrives
In other worlds, and happier home provides
For us, his offspring dear? It cannot be
But that success attends him; if mishap,
He’d have returned by now, with fury driven
By his avenger, since no place like this
Can fit his punishment, or their revenge.
I think I feel new strength within me rise,
Wings growing, and dominion given me large
Beyond this deep; whatever draws me on,
Either sympathy, or some connatural force,
Powerful at greatest distance to unite,
With secret amity, things of like kind
By secretest conveyance. You, my shade
Inseparable, must follow where I go:
For Death from Sin no power can separate.
But lest the difficulty of passing back
Should stay his return, perhaps, across this gulf
Impassable, impervious, let us try
Adventurous work, yet to your power and mine
Not unagreeable: to found a path
Over this main from Hell to that new world
Where Satan now prevails, a monument
Of merit high to all the infernal host,
Easing their passage hence, for intercourse
Or transmigration, as their lot shall lead.
Nor can I miss the way, so strongly drawn
By this new-felt attraction and instinct.”
To whom the meager Shadow soon replied:
“Go where your fate and inclination strong
Lead you; I shall not lag behind, nor miss
The way, with you to lead; such scent I draw
Of carnage, prey innumerable, and taste
The savor of death from all things there that live.
Nor in the work that you now undertake
Shall I be wanting, but give equal aid.”
So saying, with delight he sniffed the smell
Of mortal change on Earth. As when a flock
Of ravenous fowl, though many a league remote,
Against the day of battle, to a field
Where armies lie encamped come flying, lured
By scent of living carcasses designed
For death the following day in bloody fight:
So the grim Shape caught scent, and lifted high
His nostril wide into the murky air,
Keen-scented for his quarry from so far.
Then both from out Hell’s gates into the waste
Wide anarchy of Chaos, damp and dark,
Flew several ways, with power (their power was great)
Hovering upon the waters; what they met,
Solid or slimy, as in raging sea
Tossed up and down, together crowded, drove
From each side, shoaling toward the mouth of Hell:
As when two polar winds, blowing adverse
Upon the Cronian Sea, together drive
Mountains of ice that stop the imagined way
Beyond Petsora eastward to the rich
Cathayan coast. The aggregated soil
Death with his mace petrific, cold and dry,
As with a trident struck, and fixed as firm
As Delos, floating once; the rest his look
Bound with Gorgonian rigor not to move,
And with asphaltic slime; broad as the gate,
Deep to the roots of Hell, the gathered beach
They fastened, and the mole immense worked on
Over the foaming deep, high-arched, a bridge
Of length prodigious, joining to the wall
Immovable of this now fenceless world,
Forfeit to Death; from here a passage broad,
Smooth, easy, unobstructed, down to Hell.
So, if great things to small may be compared,
Xerxes, the liberty of Greece to yoke,
From Susa, his Memnonian palace high,
Came to the sea, and over Hellespont
Bridging his way, Europe with Asia joined,
And scourged with many a stroke the indignant waves.
Now had they brought the work, by wondrous art
Pontifical, a ridge of pendent rock,
Over the vexed abyss, following the track
Of Satan, to the selfsame place where he
First lighted from his wing, and landed safe
From out of Chaos on the outside bare
Of this round world. With pins of adamant
And chains they made all fast, too fast they made
And durable; and now in little space
The confines met of empyrean Heaven
And of this world, and on the left hand Hell
With long reach interposed; three separate ways
In sight, to each of these three places led.
And now their way to Earth they had descried,
Toward Paradise first tending, when, behold!
Satan, in likeness of an angel bright,
Between the Centaur and the Scorpion steering
His zenith, while the sun in Aries rose.
Disguised he came, but those his children dear
Their parent soon discerned, though in disguise.
He, after Eve’s seduction, slunk unnoticed
Into the wood close by, and, changing shape
To observe the sequel, saw his guileful act
By Eve, though all unknowing, seconded
Upon her husband; saw their shame that sought
Vain coverings; but when he saw descend
The Son of God to judge them, terrified
He fled, not hoping to escape, but shun
The present, fearing, guilty, what his wrath
Might suddenly inflict; that past, returned
By night, and, listening where the hapless pair
Sat in their sad discourse and various plaint,
Learned there his own doom, which he took to mean
Not instant, but of future time. With joy
And tidings laden, now he made for Hell,
And at the brink of Chaos, near the foot
Of this new wondrous span, unlooked-for, met
Who came to meet him there, his offspring dear.
Great joy was at their meeting, and at sight
Of that stupendous bridge his joy increased.
Long he stood admiring, till Sin, his fair
Enchanting daughter, thus the silence broke:
“O parent, these are your majestic deeds,
Your trophies, which you view as not your own;
You are their author and prime architect:
For I no sooner in my heart divined
(My heart, which by a secret harmony
Still moves with yours, joined in connection sweet)
That you on Earth had prospered, which your looks
Now also evidence, but straight I felt,
Though distant from you worlds between, yet felt
That I must follow you, with this your son;
Such fatal consequence unites us three.
Hell could no longer hold us in her bounds,
Nor this unvoyageable gulf obscure
Keep us from following your glorious track.
You have achieved our liberty, confined
Within Hell’s gates till now; you gave us power
To fortify this far, and overlay
With this portentous bridge the dark abyss.
Yours now is all this world; your valor won
What your hands did not build; your wisdom gained
With profit what war lost, and fully avenged
Our loss in Heaven; here you shall reign as king,
Which there you did not; there let him rule as victor,
As battle has adjudged, from this new world
Retiring, by his own doom alienated,
And henceforth share the monarchy with you
Of all things, parted by the empyreal bounds,
His foursquare realm, from your orbicular world,
Or try you, now more dangerous to his throne.”
To whom the Prince of Darkness gladly answered:
“Fair daughter, and you, son and grandchild both,
High proof you now have given that you’re the race
Of Satan (for I glory in the name,
Antagonist of Heaven’s almighty King),
And amply have earned reward from me, from all
The infernal empire, that so near Heaven’s door
With triumph have met triumph, matching mine
With this your glorious work, and made one realm
Hell and this world, one realm, one continent
Of easy thoroughfare. Therefore, while I
Descend through darkness, on your road, with ease,
To my associate powers, to let them know
Of these successes, and with them rejoice,
You two this way, among those numerous orbs,
All yours, right down to Paradise descend;
There dwell and reign in bliss; from there on Earth
Dominion exercise, and in the air,
Chiefly on Man, sole lord of all declared;
Him first make sure your thrall, and lastly kill.
My substitutes I send you, and create
Plenipotent on Earth, of matchless might
Issuing from me: on your joint vigor now
My hold of this new kingdom all depends,
Through Sin to Death exposed by my exploit.
If your joint power prevails, the affairs of Hell
Need fear no detriment. Go, and be strong.”
So saying, he dismissed them; they with speed
Their course through thickest constellations held,
Spreading their bane; the blasted stars looked wan,
And planets, planet-struck, real eclipse
Then suffered. The other way Satan went down
The causeway to Hell gate; on either side
Chaos, divided, built across, cried out,
And with rebounding surge the bars assailed,
That scorned his indignation. Through the gate,
Wide open and unguarded, Satan passed,
And all about found desolate; for those
Appointed to sit there had left their charge,
Flown to the upper world; the rest were all
Far to the inland withdrawn, about the walls
Of Pandaemonium, city and proud seat
Of Lucifer, so called by allusion
To that bright star to which they likened Satan.
There kept the legions watch, while the great lords
In council sat, uneasy what mischance
Might intercept their emperor, sent out; so he,
Departing, gave command, and they obeyed.
As when the Tartar from his Russian foe
By Astrakhan over the snowy plains
Retires, or Bactrian Sophy from the horns
Of Turkish crescent leaves all waste beyond
The realm of Aladule, in his retreat
To Tauris or Casbeen: so these, the late
Heaven-banished host, left desert utmost Hell
Many a dark league, drawn in to careful watch
Round their metropolis, and now expecting
Each hour their great adventurer from the search
Of foreign worlds. He through the midst, unmarked,
In show a common angel, militant,
Of lowest order, passed; and from the door
Of that Plutonian hall, invisible,
Ascended his high throne, which, canopied
With richest tapestry, at the upper end
Was placed in regal luster. Down a while
He sat, and round about him saw unseen;
At last, as from a cloud, his radiant head
And shape star-bright appeared, or brighter, clad
With what permissive glory since his fall
Was left him, or false glitter. All amazed
At that so sudden blaze, the Stygian throng
Turned all their gaze, and whom they wished beheld,
Their mighty chief returned: loud was the acclaim.
Forth rushed in haste the great consulting peers,
Raised from their dark divan, and with like joy
Approached with congratulations; who with hand
Silence, and with these words attention, won:
“Thrones, Dominations, Princedoms, Virtues, Powers,
For in possession such, not only of right,
I call you and declare you now, returned
Successful beyond hope, to lead you forth
Triumphant out of this infernal pit,
Abominable, accursed, the house of woe,
And dungeon of our tyrant. Now possess,
As lords, a spacious world, to our native Heaven
Little inferior, by my adventure hard
With peril great achieved. Too long to tell
What I have done, what suffered, with what pain
Voyaged the unreal, vast, unbounded deep
Of horrible confusion, over which
By Sin and Death a broad way now is paved
To expedite your glorious march; but I
Toiled through my unknown passage, forced to ride
The intractable abyss, plunged in the womb
Of unoriginal Night and Chaos wild,
That, jealous of their secrets, fiercely opposed
My journey strange, with clamorous uproar
Protesting Fate supreme; then how I found
The new-created world, which fame in Heaven
Long had foretold, a fabric wonderful
Of absolute perfection; in it Man
Placed in a paradise, by our exile
Made happy. Him by fraud I have seduced
From his Creator; and, the more to increase
Your wonder, with an apple! He, at this
Offended (worth your laughter), has given up
Both his beloved Man and all his world
To Sin and Death a prey, and so to us,
Without our hazard, labor, or alarm,
To range in, and to dwell, and over Man
To rule, as over all he should have ruled.
It’s true that he has judged me too, or rather
Not me, but the brute Serpent in whose shape
Man I deceived: the part that falls to me
Is enmity, which he will put between
Me and mankind; I am to bruise his heel;
His seed, at no set time, shall bruise my head.
A world, who would not purchase with a bruise,
Or much more grievous pain? You have the account
Of my performance: what remains, you gods,
But up, and enter now into full bliss?”
So having said, a while he stood, expecting
Their universal shout and high applause
To fill his ear, when, contrary, he hears
On all sides, from innumerable tongues,
A dismal universal hiss, the sound
Of public scorn. He wondered, but not long
Had leisure, wondering at himself now more:
He felt his face grow drawn, and sharp, and spare,
His arms clung to his ribs, his legs entwining
Each other, till, his footing gone, he fell,
A monstrous serpent on his belly prone,
Reluctant, but in vain: a greater power
Now ruled him, punished in the shape he sinned,
According to his doom. He would have spoken,
But hiss for hiss returned with forked tongue
To forked tongue; for now were all transformed
Alike, to serpents all, as accessories
To his bold riot. Dreadful was the din
Of hissing through the hall, thick swarming now
With intertwining monsters, head and tail,
Scorpion and asp, and amphisbaena dire,
Cerastes horned, hydrus, and ellops drear,
And dipsas (not so thick swarmed once the soil
Bedropped with blood of Gorgon, or the isle
Ophiusa); but greatest he, at the center,
Now dragon grown, larger than whom the sun
Engendered in the Pythian vale from slime,
Huge Python; and his power no less he seemed
Above the rest still to retain. They all
Followed him, issuing forth to the open field,
Where all yet left of that revolted rout,
Heaven-fallen, in station stood or just array,
Sublime with expectation when to see
In triumph issuing forth their glorious chief.
They saw, but other sight instead: a crowd
Of ugly serpents. Horror on them fell,
And horrid sympathy; for what they saw
They felt themselves now changing; down their arms,
Down fell both spear and shield, down they as fast,
And the dire hiss renewed, and the dire form
Caught by contagion, like in punishment
As in their crime. So was the applause they meant
Turned to exploding hiss, triumph to shame
Cast on themselves from their own mouths. There stood
A grove close by, sprung up with this their change,
By will of him above, to aggravate
Their penance, laden with fair fruit, like that
Which grew in Paradise, the bait of Eve
Used by the tempter. On that prospect strange
Their earnest eyes they fixed, imagining
For one forbidden tree a multitude
Now risen, to work them further woe or shame;
Yet, parched with scalding thirst and hunger fierce,
Though sent to cheat them, they could not abstain,
But on they rolled in heaps, and, up the trees
Climbing, sat thicker than the snaky locks
That curled Megaera. Greedily they plucked
The fruitage fair to sight, like that which grew
Near that bituminous lake where Sodom flamed;
This more delusive, not the touch, but taste
Deceived; they, fondly thinking to allay
Their appetite with relish, instead of fruit
Chewed bitter ashes, which the offended taste
With spattering noise rejected. Often they tried,
Hunger and thirst constraining, sickened as often,
With most abhorrent loathing writhed their jaws,
With soot and cinders filled; so often they fell
Into the same illusion, not like Man,
Their conquest, who lapsed once. Thus were they plagued
And worn with famine, long and ceaseless hiss,
Till their lost shape, permitted, they resumed,
Yearly enjoined, some say, to undergo
This annual humbling certain numbered days,
To dash their pride, and joy for Man seduced.
However, some tradition they dispersed
Among the heathen they had won as spoil,
And fabled how the Serpent, whom they called
Ophion, with Eurynome (the wide-
Encroaching Eve perhaps), had first the rule
Of high Olympus, thence by Saturn driven
And Ops, before Dictaean Jove was born.
Meanwhile in Paradise the hellish pair
Too soon arrived: Sin, there in power before,
Once actual, now in body, and to dwell
Habitual resident; behind her Death
Close following pace for pace, not mounted yet
On his pale horse; to whom Sin thus began:
“Second of Satan sprung, all-conquering Death,
What say you of our empire now, though earned
With travail difficult? Is it not better far
Than still at Hell’s dark threshold to sit watch,
Unnamed, undreaded, and yourself half starved?”
To whom the Sin-born monster soon replied:
“To me, who pine with everlasting famine,
Alike is Hell, or Paradise, or Heaven;
There best, where I may meet the most of prey;
Which here, though plenteous, all too little seems
To stuff this maw, this vast and loose-skinned corpse.”
To whom the incestuous mother thus replied:
“You therefore on these herbs, and fruits, and flowers
Feed first; on each beast next, and fish, and fowl,
No homely morsels; and whatever thing
The scythe of Time mows down, devour unspared,
Till I, in Man residing through the race,
His thoughts, his looks, words, actions, all infect,
And season him your last and sweetest prey.”
This said, they went off each a separate way,
Both to destroy, or unimmortal make
All kinds, and for destruction to mature
Sooner or later; which the Almighty seeing,
From his transcendent seat the saints among,
To those bright orders uttered thus his voice:
“See with what heat these dogs of Hell advance
To waste and wreck that world below, which I
So fair and good created, and had still
Kept in that state, had not the folly of Man
Let in these wasteful Furies, who impute
Folly to me (so does the Prince of Hell
And his adherents), that with so much ease
I suffer them to enter and possess
A place so heavenly, and conniving seem
To gratify my scornful enemies,
That laugh, as if, transported with some fit
Of passion, I to them had quitted all,
At random yielded up to their misrule;
And know not that I called and drew them there,
My hellhounds, to lick up the draff and filth
Which man’s polluting sin with taint has shed
On what was pure, till, crammed and gorged, near burst
With sucked and glutted offal, at one fling
Of your victorious arm, well-pleasing Son,
Both Sin, and Death, and yawning Grave at last,
Through Chaos hurled, obstruct the mouth of Hell
Forever, and seal up his ravenous jaws.
Then Heaven and Earth, renewed, shall be made pure
To sanctity that shall receive no stain:
Till then the curse pronounced on both precedes.”
He ended, and the heavenly audience loud
Sang Hallelujah, as the sound of seas,
Through multitudes that sang: “Just are your ways,
Righteous are your decrees on all your works;
Who can extenuate you?” Next, to the Son,
Destined restorer of mankind, by whom
New Heaven and Earth shall to the ages rise,
Or down from Heaven descend. Such was their song,
While the Creator, calling forth by name
His mighty angels, gave them several charge,
As suited best with present things. The sun
Had first his precept so to move, so shine,
As might affect the earth with cold and heat
Scarce tolerable, and from the north to call
Decrepit winter, from the south to bring
Solstitial summer’s heat. To the pale moon
Her office they prescribed; to the other five
Their planetary motions and aspects,
In sextile, square, and trine, and opposite,
Of noxious efficacy, and when to join
In synod unbenign; and taught the fixed
Their influence malignant when to shower,
Which of them, rising with the sun, or falling,
Should prove tempestuous. To the winds they set
Their corners, when with bluster to confound
Sea, air, and shore; the thunder when to roll
With terror through the dark aerial hall.
Some say he bid his angels turn askance
The poles of earth twice ten degrees and more
From the sun’s axle; they with labor pushed
Oblique the central globe. Some say the sun
Was bid to turn from the equinoctial road
Like distant breadth to Taurus with the seven
Atlantic sisters, and the Spartan twins,
Up to the tropic Crab; then down at speed
By Leo, and the Virgin, and the Scales,
As deep as Capricorn, to bring in change
Of seasons to each clime; else had the spring
Perpetual smiled on earth with vernal flowers,
Equal in days and nights, except to those
Beyond the polar circles; to them day
Had shone unbenighted, while the low sun,
To recompense his distance, in their sight
Would still have ringed the horizon, and not known
East or the west, which would have kept the snow
From cold Estotiland, and south as far
Beneath Magellan. At that tasted fruit
The sun, as from Thyestean banquet, turned
His course intended; else how would the world,
Inhabited, though sinless, more than now,
Have shunned the pinching cold and scorching heat?
These changes in the heavens, though slow, produced
Like change on sea and land: sidereal blast,
Vapor, and mist, and exhalation hot,
Corrupt and pestilent. Now from the north
Of Norumbega, and the Samoed shore,
Bursting their brazen dungeon, armed with ice,
And snow, and hail, and stormy gust and squall,
Boreas and Caecias and Argestes loud
And Thrascias rend the woods and seas upturn;
With adverse blast upturns them from the south
Notus, and Afer black with thunderous clouds
From Sierra Leone; across these, as fierce,
Forth rush the Levant and the Ponent winds,
Eurus and Zephyr, with their lateral noise,
Sirocco and Libecchio. Thus began
Outrage from lifeless things; but Discord first,
Daughter of Sin, among the irrational
Death introduced through fierce antipathy:
Beast now made war with beast, and fowl with fowl,
And fish with fish; to graze the herb all leaving,
Devoured each other; nor stood much in awe
Of Man, but fled him, or with countenance grim
Glared on him passing. These were from without
The growing miseries, which Adam saw
Already in part, though hid in gloomiest shade,
To sorrow abandoned, but worse felt within,
And, in a troubled sea of passion tossed,
Thus to unburden sought with sad complaint:
“O wretched, once so happy! Is this the end
Of this new glorious world, and me, so late
The glory of that glory, now become
Accursed from blessed? Hide me from the face
Of God, whom to behold was then my height
Of happiness! Yet well, if here would end
The misery; I deserved it, and would bear
My own deservings; but this will not serve:
All that I eat or drink, or shall beget,
Is propagated curse. O voice once heard
Delightfully, ‘Increase and multiply,’
Now death to hear! For what can I increase
Or multiply but curses on my head?
Who of all ages to succeed, but, feeling
The evil on him brought by me, will curse
My head: ‘Ill fare our ancestor impure!
For this we may thank Adam!’ But his thanks
Shall be the execration; so, besides
My own that stay upon me, all from me
Shall with a fierce reflux on me redound,
On me, as on their natural center, light
Heavy, though in their place. O fleeting joys
Of Paradise, dear bought with lasting woes!
Did I request you, Maker, from my clay
To mold me Man? Did I solicit you
From darkness to promote me, or here place
In this delicious garden? As my will
Concurred not to my being, it were but right
And equal to reduce me to my dust,
Desirous to resign and render back
All I received, unable to perform
Your terms, too hard, by which I was to hold
The good I sought not. To the loss of that,
Sufficient penalty, why have you added
The sense of endless woes? Inexplicable
Your justice seems; yet, to say truth, too late
I thus contest; then should have been refused
Those terms, whatever, when they were proposed.
You did accept them; will you enjoy the good,
Then cavil at the conditions? And though God
Made you without your leave, what if your son
Prove disobedient, and, reproved, retort,
‘Why did you beget me? I did not ask it’?
Would you admit, for his contempt of you,
That proud excuse? Yet him not your election,
But natural necessity begot.
God made you by his choice, and as his own
To serve him; your reward was of his grace;
Your punishment, then, justly rests in his will.
Be it so, for I submit; his doom is fair,
That dust I am, and shall to dust return.
O welcome hour, whenever! Why delays
His hand to execute what his decree
Fixed on this day? Why do I live past it,
Why am I mocked with death, and lengthened out
To deathless pain? How gladly would I meet
Mortality, my sentence, and be earth
Insensible! How glad would lay me down
As in my mother’s lap! There I should rest
And sleep secure; his dreadful voice no more
Would thunder in my ears; no fear of worse
To me and to my offspring would torment me
With cruel expectation. Yet one doubt
Pursues me still, lest all I cannot die;
Lest that pure breath of life, the spirit of Man
Which God inspired, cannot together perish
With this corporeal clod; then, in the grave,
Or in some other dismal place, who knows
But I shall die a living death? O thought
Horrid, if true! Yet why? It was but breath
Of life that sinned: what dies but what had life
And sin? The body properly has neither.
All of me, then, shall die: let this appease
The doubt, since human reach no further knows.
For though the Lord of all be infinite,
Is his wrath also? Be it; man is not so,
But mortal doomed. How can he exercise
Wrath without end on Man, whom death must end?
Can he make deathless death? That were to make
Strange contradiction, which to God himself
Impossible is held, as argument
Of weakness, not of power. Will he draw out,
For anger’s sake, finite to infinite
In punished man, to satisfy his rigor,
Satisfied never? That were to extend
His sentence beyond dust and nature’s law,
By which all causes else, according still
To the reception of their matter, act,
Not to the extent of their own sphere. But say
That death be not one stroke, as I supposed,
Bereaving sense, but endless misery
From this day onward, which I feel begun
Both in me and without me, and so last
To perpetuity: ah me, that fear
Comes thundering back with dreadful revolution
On my defenseless head! Both Death and I
Are found eternal, and incorporate both;
Nor I on my part single: in me all
Posterity stands cursed. Fair patrimony
That I must leave you, sons! O were I able
To waste it all myself, and leave you none!
So disinherited, how would you bless
Me, now your curse! Ah, why should all mankind
For one man’s fault thus guiltless be condemned,
If guiltless? But from me what can proceed
But all corrupt, both mind and will depraved,
Not to do only, but to will the same
With me? How can they then acquitted stand
In sight of God? Him, after all disputes,
Forced, I absolve: all my evasions vain
And reasonings, though through mazes, lead me still
But to my own conviction: first and last
On me, me only, as the source and spring
Of all corruption, all the blame lights due;
So might the wrath! Vain wish! Could you support
That burden, heavier than the earth to bear,
Than all the world much heavier, though divided
With that bad woman? Thus what you desire
And what you fear alike destroys all hope
Of refuge, and concludes you miserable
Beyond all past example and future,
To Satan only like, both crime and doom.
O Conscience, into what abyss of fears
And horrors have you driven me, out of which
I find no way, from deep to deeper plunged!”
Thus Adam to himself lamented loud
Through the still night, not now, as before man fell,
Wholesome and cool and mild, but with black air
Accompanied, with damps and dreadful gloom,
Which to his evil conscience represented
All things with double terror. On the ground
Outstretched he lay, on the cold ground, and often
Cursed his creation; Death as often accused
Of tardy execution, since pronounced
The day of his offense. “Why does Death not come,”
He said, “with one thrice-acceptable stroke
To end me? Shall Truth fail to keep her word,
Justice divine not hasten to be just?
But Death comes not when called; Justice divine
Does not quicken her pace for prayers or cries.
O woods, O fountains, hillocks, dales, and bowers,
With far other echo I taught your shades
To answer, and resound far other song!”
When sad Eve saw him thus afflicted, she,
Desolate where she sat, approaching near,
On his fierce passion tried her gentlest words;
But her with stern regard he thus repelled:
“Out of my sight, you serpent! That name best
Befits you, leagued with him, yourself as false
And hateful; nothing’s lacking, but that your shape,
Like his, and color serpentine, may show
Your inward fraud, to warn all creatures from you
Henceforth, lest that too heavenly form, pretended
To hellish falsehood, snare them. But for you
I had persisted happy, had not your pride
And wandering vanity, when least was safe,
Rejected my forewarning, and disdained
Not to be trusted, longing to be seen
Though by the Devil himself, too proudly thinking
To overreach him; but, the Serpent meeting,
Fooled and beguiled; by him you, I by you,
To trust you from my side, imagined wise,
Constant, mature, proof against all assaults,
And understood not all was but a show,
Rather than solid virtue; all but a rib
Crooked by nature, bent, as now appears,
More to the part sinister, from me drawn;
Well if thrown out, as supernumerary
To my just number found. O why did God,
Creator wise, that peopled highest Heaven
With spirits masculine, create at last
This novelty on earth, this fair defect
Of nature, and not fill the world at once
With men, as angels, without feminine,
Or find some other way to generate
Mankind? This mischief had not then befallen,
And more that shall befall, innumerable
Disturbances on earth through female snares,
And close conjunction with this sex: for either
He never shall find out fit mate, but such
As some misfortune brings him, or mistake;
Or whom he wishes most shall seldom gain
Through her perverseness, but shall see her gained
By one far worse; or if she love, withheld
By parents; or his happiest choice too late
Shall meet, already linked and wedlock-bound
To a fell adversary, his hate or shame:
Which infinite calamity shall cause
To human life, and household peace confound.”
He said no more, and turned from her; but Eve,
Not so repulsed, with tears that kept on flowing,
And tresses all disordered, at his feet
Fell humble, and, embracing them, besought
His peace, and thus continued her lament:
“Do not forsake me so, Adam! Witness, Heaven,
What love sincere and reverence in my heart
I bear you, and unwittingly have offended,
Unhappily deceived! Your suppliant
I beg, and clasp your knees; do not deprive me
Of what I live by: your gentle looks, your aid,
Your counsel in this uttermost distress,
My only strength and stay. Forlorn of you,
Where shall I turn for refuge, where subsist?
While yet we live, scarce one short hour perhaps,
Between us two let there be peace, both joining,
As joined in injuries, in one enmity
Against a foe by doom expressly assigned us,
That cruel Serpent. Do not exercise
Your hatred for this misery befallen
On me, already lost, on me, more wretched
Than you are now. Both of us sinned, but you
Against God only; I, God and yourself,
And to the place of judgment will return,
There with my cries importune Heaven, that all
The sentence, from your head removed, may light
On me, sole cause to you of all this woe,
Me, me only, just object of his ire.”
She ended weeping; and her lowly plight,
Immovable till peace obtained, from fault
Acknowledged and deplored, in Adam wrought
Commiseration. Soon his heart relented
Toward her, his life so late and sole delight,
Now at his feet submissive in distress,
Creature so fair his reconcilement seeking,
His counsel, whom she had displeased, his aid:
As one disarmed, his anger all he lost,
And thus with peaceful words upraised her soon:
“Unwary, and too desirous, as before,
So now, of what you do not know, who wish
The punishment all on yourself! Alas,
Bear your own first, ill able to sustain
His full wrath, whose least part you feel as yet,
And my displeasure bear so ill. If prayers
Could alter high decrees, I to that place
Would speed before you, and be louder heard,
That on my head all might be visited,
Your frailty and your weaker sex forgiven,
To me committed, and by me exposed.
But rise; let us no more contend, nor blame
Each other, blamed enough elsewhere, but strive
In offices of love how we may lighten
Each other’s burden in our share of woe;
Since this day’s death, pronounced, if I see right,
Will prove no sudden but a slow-paced evil,
A long day’s dying, to augment our pain,
And to our seed (O hapless seed!) passed down.”
To whom thus Eve, recovering heart, replied:
“Adam, by sad experiment I know
How little weight my words with you can find,
Found so erroneous, and then, by just event,
Found so unfortunate; nevertheless,
Restored by you, vile as I am, to place
Of new acceptance, hopeful to regain
Your love, the sole contentment of my heart,
Living or dying from you I will not hide
What thoughts in my unquiet breast have risen,
Tending to some relief of our extremes,
Or end, though sharp and sad, yet tolerable,
As in our evils, and of easier choice.
If care for our descendants vex us most,
Who must be born to certain woe, devoured
By Death at last (and miserable it is
To be to others cause of misery,
Our own begotten, and of our loins to bring
Into this cursed world a woeful race,
That after wretched life must be at last
Food for so foul a monster), in your power
It lies, yet before conception, to prevent
The race unblessed, as yet unborn to being.
Childless you are; then childless stay: so Death
Shall be cheated of his glut, and with us two
Be forced to satisfy his ravenous maw.
But if you judge it hard and difficult,
Conversing, looking, loving, to abstain
From love’s due rites, nuptial embraces sweet,
And with desire to languish without hope
Before the present object, languishing
With like desire, which would be misery
And torment less than none of what we dread;
Then, both ourselves and seed at once to free
From what we fear for both, let us make short:
Let us seek Death, or, he not found, supply
With our own hands his office on ourselves.
Why do we stand here shivering under fears
That show no end but death, and have the power,
Of many ways to die the shortest choosing,
Destruction with destruction to destroy?”
She ended here, or vehement despair
Broke off the rest; so much of death her thoughts
Had entertained, as dyed her cheeks with pale.
But Adam, by such counsel nothing swayed,
To better hopes his more attentive mind
Laboring had raised, and thus to Eve replied:
“Eve, your contempt of life and pleasure seems
To argue in you something more sublime
And excellent than what your mind contemns;
But self-destruction, therefore sought, refutes
That excellence thought in you, and implies,
Not your contempt, but anguish and regret
For loss of life and pleasure overloved.
Or if you covet death, as utmost end
Of misery, so thinking to evade
The penalty pronounced, doubt not but God
Has armed his vengeful ire more wisely than
To be forestalled; much more I fear lest death,
So snatched, will not exempt us from the pain
We are by doom to pay; rather, such acts
Of contumacy will provoke the Highest
To make death in us live. Then let us seek
Some safer resolution, which, I think,
I have in view, calling to mind with heed
Part of our sentence, that your seed shall bruise
The Serpent’s head: piteous amends, unless
Is meant, as I conjecture, our grand foe,
Satan, who in the Serpent has contrived
Against us this deceit. To crush his head
Would be revenge indeed, which will be lost
By death brought on ourselves, or childless days
Resolved, as you propose; and so our foe
Shall then escape his doom ordained, and we
Instead shall double ours upon our heads.
Let no more then be said of violence
Against ourselves, and willful barrenness,
That cuts us off from hope, and savors only
Rancor and pride, impatience and despite,
Reluctance against God and his just yoke
Laid on our necks. Remember with what mild
And gracious temper he both heard and judged,
Without wrath or reviling. We expected
Immediate dissolution, which we thought
Was meant by death that day; when, behold, to you
Pains only in childbearing were foretold,
And bringing forth, soon recompensed with joy,
Fruit of your womb. On me the curse aslant
Glanced on the ground: with labor I must earn
My bread; what harm? Idleness had been worse;
My labor will sustain me; and lest cold
Or heat should injure us, his timely care
Has, unrequested, given, and his hands
Clothed us unworthy, pitying while he judged;
How much more, if we pray to him, will his ear
Be open, and his heart to pity incline,
And teach us further by what means to shun
The inclement seasons, rain, ice, hail, and snow,
Which now the sky with various face begins
To show us on this mountain, while the winds
Blow moist and keen, shattering the graceful locks
Of these fair spreading trees; which bids us seek
Some better shelter, some better warmth to cherish
Our limbs benumbed, before this daily star
Leaves cold the night; how we, his gathered beams
Reflected, may with withered matter kindle,
Or by collision of two bodies grind
The rubbed air into fire, as lately clouds,
Jostling, or pushed by winds, rude in their shock,
Strike out slant lightning, whose cross flame, driven down,
Kindles the gummy bark of fir or pine,
And sends a comfortable heat from far,
Which might supply the sun: such fire to use,
And what may else be remedy or cure
To evils which our own misdeeds have wrought,
He will instruct us, praying, and of grace
Beseeching him; so that we need not fear
To pass this life with ease enough, sustained
By him with many comforts, till we end
In dust, our final rest and native home.
What better can we do than, to the place
Returning where he judged us, prostrate fall
Before him reverent, and there confess
Humbly our faults, and pardon beg, with tears
Watering the ground, and with our sighs the air
Frequenting, sent from hearts contrite, in sign
Of sorrow unfeigned, and humiliation meek?
Undoubtedly he will relent, and turn
From his displeasure; in whose look serene,
When angry most he seemed and most severe,
What else but favor, grace, and mercy shone?”
So spoke our father penitent; nor Eve
Felt less remorse. They promptly, to the place
Returning where he judged them, prostrate fell
Before him reverent, and both confessed
Humbly their faults, and pardon begged, with tears
Watering the ground, and with their sighs the air
Frequenting, sent from hearts contrite, in sign
Of sorrow unfeigned, and humiliation meek.

blocks.p: Vicegerent (56). A deputy who rules with delegated authority; the Father commits all judgment to the Son [John 5:22].
The three sentences (175–208). Milton follows the curses of Genesis almost word for word [Gen. 3:14–19].
Her seed shall bruise your head (181). Read since early Christian times as the first promise of Christ’s victory over Satan [Gen. 3:15].

Satan fall like lightning … captivity led captive (184–188). Christ’s words and Paul’s: Satan as “prince of the power of the air,” stripped and led in triumph [Luke 10:18; Eph. 2:2; Col. 2:15; Eph. 4:8]; and the promise to tread Satan under foot [Rom. 16:20].
form of servant … washed his servants’ feet (214–215). Christ took “the form of a servant” and washed his disciples’ feet [Phil. 2:7; John 13:5].
robe of righteousness (222). Righteousness pictured as a garment God puts on the redeemed [Isa. 61:10].
Cronian Sea … Petsora … Cathayan coast (290–293). The Arctic Ocean; the Pechora River in northern Russia; and China (Cathay), the goal of the hoped-for Northeast Passage.
mace petrific (294). A club that turns things to stone.
Delos (296). The Aegean island that floated loose until, in myth, it was fixed in place for Apollo’s birth.
Gorgonian (297). Like the Gorgon Medusa, whose look turned the living to stone.
mole (300). A massive causeway or pier of stone.

Xerxes (307). The Persian king who bridged the Hellespont with boats to invade Greece, and had the sea whipped when a storm broke his bridge; Susa was his capital, called Memnonian after the legendary king Memnon.
Pontifical (313). Bridge-building (Latin pontifex, “bridge-maker”), with a glance at the papacy.
Between the Centaur and the Scorpion (328). Satan flies through Sagittarius and Scorpio, the part of the sky opposite the sun in Aries, so as to keep to the night side.
Lucifer (425). “Light-bearer,” the morning star, applied to Satan from [Isa. 14:12].

Astrakhan … Aladule … Tauris or Casbeen (432–436). Tartars retreating from the Russians, and the Persian Shah (the Sophy) falling back before the Turks, laying waste Armenia as he withdraws to Tabriz or Qazvin.
Plutonian (444). Belonging to Pluto, god of the underworld.
divan (457). A Turkish council of state.
unoriginal Night (477). Night that had no beginning, being older than creation.

amphisbaena … dipsas (524–526). Serpents from Lucan’s catalog of Libyan snakes: the two-headed amphisbaena, the horned cerastes, the water snake hydrus, the ellops, and the dipsas, whose bite brought burning thirst.
blood of Gorgon … Ophiusa (527–528). Libya, where snakes sprang from the drops of Medusa’s blood; Ophiusa, “snake island,” in the Mediterranean.
Python (531). The huge serpent bred from the mud after the Flood, slain by Apollo at Delphi.
exploding (546). In its Latin sense: hissing a performer off the stage.
Megaera (560). One of the Furies, whose hair was snakes.
that bituminous lake where Sodom flamed (562). The Dead Sea, where the “apples of Sodom” were said to look fair but turn to ashes in the mouth.

Ophion with Eurynome (581). In a Greek myth, the serpent Ophion and Eurynome (“wide-ruling”) held Olympus before Saturn and Ops (Cronos and Rhea) drove them out; Milton reads them as a pagan memory of Satan and Eve; Jove was born on Mount Dicte in Crete.
pale horse (590). Death’s mount in [Rev. 6:8].
draff (630). Dregs, refuse.
Just are your ways (643). The angels’ song echoes the hymns of Revelation [Rev. 15:3; 19:1–6].
sextile, square, and trine, and opposite (659). Astrological aspects, angles of 60, 90, 120 and 180 degrees between planets, thought to work harm or good; a “synod” (661) is a conjunction.
Some say … Some say (668–671). Two explanations of the seasons: either the earth’s axis was tilted (as Copernicus held), or the sun’s path was angled (as Ptolemy held).
seven Atlantic sisters … Spartan twins … tropic Crab (673–675). The Pleiades in Taurus, Castor and Pollux in Gemini, and Cancer; then Leo, Virgo, Libra and Capricorn.
Estotiland … Magellan (686–687). Northern Labrador, and the Strait of Magellan at the tip of South America.
Thyestean banquet (688). The sun turned back in horror when Atreus served Thyestes the flesh of his own sons.
Norumbega … Samoed shore (696). New England and Maine, and the Arctic coast of Siberia.

Boreas … Libecchio (699–706). Winds of every quarter: north and northeast (Boreas, Caecias, Argestes, Thrascias), south (Notus, Afer, the African wind), east and west (Levant and Ponent, Eurus and Zephyr), southeast and southwest (Sirocco, Libecchio).
Increase and multiply (730). God’s first blessing on mankind [Gen. 1:28].
Did I request you, Maker (743). Compare the clay questioning the potter [Isa. 45:9]; Mary Shelley took these lines as the epigraph of Frankenstein.
sinister (886). Left (its Latin sense), with a pun on evil; Eve was said to be made from a rib on Adam’s left side, an extra one beyond his “just number.”
contumacy (1027). Stubborn defiance of authority.
